title: Short Stuff: Happy Foods!
summary: Short Stuff episode "Happy Foods" (June 2022). Josh and guest host Jerry (in for Dave) revisit an old HowStuffWorks-era article by Josh on how foods affect mood. They distinguish "happy foods" (direct physiological effects on mood through neurotransmitters) from "comfort foods" (psychological and nostalgic associations). They cover excitatory (norepinephrine, epinephrine) and inhibitory (serotonin, GABA) neurotransmitters and the need for balance; tryptophan and vitamin B6 as serotonin precursors (turkey, bananas); the Krebs cycle and GABA made from glutamate/glutamine (sesame, sunflower seeds, pork, beef); a 2005 Cornell survey of comfort foods showing women seek sugary foods and men seek soup and steak; and DHA (docosahexaenoic acid), the most abundant fat in the brain, found in fish, with a Taiwan-linked correlation between fish eating and lower depression. The hosts also joke about the script's errors and the lack of a prepared intro.

segments.title: Opening banter and origin of the script
segments.summary: Josh introduces the Short Stuff happy foods edition, notes it is an old article he wrote for HowStuffWorks, and jokes about its wording, including a garbled line about the Krebs cycle.

segments.title: Happy foods vs. comfort foods
segments.summary: The hosts define happy foods as those that affect mood through direct physiological action, and comfort foods as those that affect mood through psychological associations.

segments.title: Excitatory and inhibitory neurotransmitters
segments.summary: Norepinephrine and epinephrine are described as excitatory, serotonin as inhibitory and calming. The hosts say the best mood comes from a balance between the two types, and that the body builds neurotransmitters from nutrients in food.

segments.title: Serotonin, tryptophan and B vitamins
segments.summary: Serotonin is called a happy neurotransmitter. Tryptophan, found in foods such as turkey and bananas, can cross the blood-brain barrier and is converted to serotonin in the brain. Vitamin B6 is needed to make serotonin fully.

segments.title: GABA and glutamine from food
segments.summary: GABA, sometimes called nature's Valium, is made from glutamine, an amino acid found in foods such as sesame and sunflower seeds, pork and beef. The hosts say it helps with sleep and relaxation.

segments.title: Comfort food preferences and a 2005 Cornell survey
segments.summary: Josh and Jerry share their personal comfort foods. The hosts cite a 2005 Cornell survey of nearly 300 men and women, which found women seek sugary foods more and men seek soup and steak. They note the claim about evolutionary advantage sounds dubious.

segments.title: DHA, fish and depression
segments.summary: DHA, the most abundant fat in the human brain, is found in fish and shellfish. A correlation was noted between high fish consumption in places like Taiwan and lower depression rates, though the hosts stress this does not prove causation.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts joke about the episode and wrap up, and the standard closing credits about the show's production company are read.
